description: This course combines the study of the structure of national, state, and local U.S. government with an overview of the principals of market economics. Students will examine the general structure and functions of the U.S. systems of government, the roles and responsibilities of citizens to participate in the political process, and the relationship of the individual to the law and legal system. Students will become informed citizens after taking this course.
fulfills_text: 1 credit Civics/American Government required (p.12)

description: This course aims to familiarize students with our nation's legal system. Students will acquire practical information and problem-solving skills that are necessary for a full and productive roll in our Democracy. Topics will include: An introduction to our Legal System, Criminal Law, Torts, Law and Politics, Family Law and Individual Rights and Liberties (Constitutional Law).

Sociology is the social science that studies human society and social behavior. This course will teach a theoretical paradigm approach to analyze society in a way that allows the development of the sociological imagination. This is a tool that will promote understanding in both self and societal applications. Knowledge and awareness are powerful indicators of success. The topics we will cover and analyze include Culture Diversity, Conformity and Adaptation, Social Structure, Socialization and Social Stratification.

Modern U.S. History courses examine the history of the United States from the Civil War or Reconstruction era (some courses begin at a later period) through the present time. These courses typically include a historical review of political, military, scientific, and social developments.
fulfills_text: Required to Graduate

description: In this course, we will align with the freshmen English course in a collaborative effort to explore the emergence of Western Civilization from the early Greek Civilization through the Enlightenment. We will improve our global awareness through map activities, utilize primary sources, strengthen vocabulary and overall reading comprehension. We will continue to build on the skills of identifying bias and determining its intention as well as argumentative writing.
fulfills_text: 1 credit World History required (p.12)

description: In this course, students will explore the complexities of the human mind by examining the science behind why we think, feel, and do. Students will experience the evolution of psychology through the early schools of thought, major branches, and core theories that guide contemporary perspectives. As students consider the broad influence of psychology on their perceptions, emotions, and everyday choices, they will acknowledge the idea that, in the human experience, “psychology is everywhere.”
notes: Psychology (Hon) receives additional five GPA points (p.11)

description: French 1 is a foundational, full-year high school course that introduces students to the French language and Francophone cultures. It develops basic proficiency in listening, speaking, reading, and writing through real-life contexts. Students learn essential vocabulary, foundational grammar (like present tense verbs), and cultural traditions from around the world.

French II focuses on three core modes of communication: interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational. Students transition from basic, memorized phrases to forming more complex, spontaneous sentences.
prerequisites: French I

description: French Conversation and Culture courses provide students with an introduction to the French language and the culture(s) of French-speaking people, placing greater emphasis on speaking and listening skills while deemphasizing writing and reading the language.

Spanish II courses build upon skills developed in Spanish I, extending students’ ability to understand and express themselves in Spanish and increasing their vocabulary. Typically, students learn how to engage in discourse for informative or social purposes, write expressions or passages that show understanding of sentence construction and the rules of grammar, and comprehend the language when spoken slowly. Students usually explore the customs, history, and art forms of Spanish-speaking people to deepen their understanding of the culture(s).
prerequisites: Spanish I

description: VHS offers a large selection of over 250 courses which may be taken for elective credit only. Students are required to be in the library during their scheduled virtual high school block every day. These are highly rigorous courses and require more hours than a traditional class. Students are required to do classwork during school vacations for VHS classes. Students may elect to take a VHS class outside of the school day if they are fully enrolled at BUHS with a full schedule. In this case the VHS class would be added to a period ten assignment. As a student you must be self-disciplined, highly motivated, and make time to log into your class on a daily basis. For a complete listing of available courses check out the VHS website at www.vhslearning.org – on the menu click VHS catalog. Students will not be scheduled for VHS courses until the application process is complete. Application process: 1. Obtain an application in the counseling office and fill it out. There is an application form on the BUHS school website as well. 2. Turn the completed application into the VHS Coordinator: Allison Cram (email: acram@wsesdvt.org) 3. Interview with VHS Coordinator. 4. Additional Steps are required for VHS Flex Class (see above)

description: Students in this course will read, analyze, and create literature in three different genres: poetry, short fiction, and personal essay. There is an emphasis on exploring the idea generation and drafting stages of the creative process, building confidence with sharing and providing feedback on creative work, using figurative language, and exploring different narrative structures. Students who enroll should be prepared to share their work in large and small group settings and provide constructive feedback on the work of their peers. Students should also be prepared to read and analyze published works in order to expand and refine their own writing skills. This course assumes grade-level reading, writing, speaking, and problem-solving skills. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any other English course.

description: Despite being closely related to comic books, the study of Graphic Novels is in fact a serious look at literature, storytelling, story analysis and story creation. This increasingly popular style encompasses any genre and has become relevant in the world of today’s students. This course is being specifically designed to offer more English electives to 9th and 10th graders. There will be substantial choice reading in the class as well as revisiting classics in the Graphic Novel format. This class will also explore creativity and technology as students develop their own Graphic novels, with or without the help of tech programs. Titles may include: To Kill a Mockingbird, The Odyssey, Maus and Maus II, Persepolis, works by William Shakespeare, Long Way Down. This course assumes grade-level reading, writing, speaking, and problem-solving skills. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any other English course.

description: When we think of the magic of theatre, we often think about the performances of the actors, the lights, the costumes, or the sets–but none of those things are possible without the work of the playwright. In this course, we will explore the process that goes into writing a play. We’ll begin by examining what a playwright actually does, while exploring and addressing preconceived notions students may have regarding playwriting. We’ll consider where playwrights find their ideas, and how they employ character and conflict to create a piece of theatre. As part of the learning process, students will write and workshop monologues and short plays with their colleagues, learning how to give and receive peer-to-peer feedback. And, as plays are meant to be staged, not read, students will also perform their work in class, both on their own and with their colleagues. This course assumes grade-level reading, writing, speaking, and problem-solving skills. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any other English course.
prerequisites: For students in Grade 10 - Successful completion English 1 or English 1 Advanced
offering_note: Schedule as printed: Semester / Spring Only

description: This course requires students to submit a completed course contract and to complete substantial pre-course assignments. Students who complete this course are also required to take the corresponding Advanced Placement English Literature and Composition exam in May. This course is designed according to guidelines set by the Advanced Placement Program of the College Board. It emphasizes critical reading of literature and advanced composition. The class is challenging and will take greater time and effort than other electives. Students who choose it should have strong English skills and thorough preparation for literary studies. Readings may include works by William Shakespeare, Mary Shelley, Zora Neale Hurston, Ralph Ellison, Charles Dickens, Emily Bronte, Kurt Vonnegut, Chinua Achebe, Margaret Atwood, among others, and major poets of England and America, among others. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English

description: This course is available for English credit for students in grades 11-12. The study of journalism is an effective way to develop both reading and writing skills, the foundations of literacy. The two underlying beliefs of this intensive journalistic writing course are as follows: (1) a command of clear, concise language leads to effective written and spoken communication; and (2) students who take an intensive journalistic writing course learn skills useful in any field of endeavor. Through writing, reading, viewing, and discussing, students in this course will learn the principles of ethical journalism, interviewing techniques, news writing, editing, and newspaper design. In addition, students will read and discuss the work of professional journalists. Class members will contribute to the student newspaper, THE BRATTLEBORO BEACON. This course is a prerequisite for Advanced Journalism. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English.
fulfills_text: This course is available for English credit for students in grades 11-12.

description: This course is an advanced offering of Intro to Journalism. The goal of this class is to apply the journalism skills learned previously to other media. Through hands-on experience, students in this course will continue to develop their knowledge of the principles of ethical journalism, interviewing techniques, news writing, editing, and newspaper design. In addition, students will read and discuss the work of other journalists. . MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: English 1 or English 1 Advanced, a second course in English, and successful completion of Introduction to Journalism (Journalism 1)

description: This course is intended for students interested in reading non-fiction and fiction stories of adventure (stories of survival, both physical and psychological). The goal is to heighten the student’s interest in reading more and varied selections. Students will also view films with themes related to the reading, and write reviews, essays, etc. Longer titles include The Things They Carried, Unbroken, and Into Thin Air. Expect reading homework most nights.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English
notes: (THIS COURSE ALTERNATES WITH SPORTS LITERATURE) MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.

description: This course is an opportunity to take English 3 or 4 for both high school and college credit. This course consists of two major areas of study: writing and literature. The writing area is designed to review and improve writing skills. The other focus of the course, literature, will enable students to study standard literary works (both traditional and non-traditional selections) which are organized thematically. Vocabulary study is also stressed. Readings include titles such as Lord of the Flies, Othello, Animal Farm, Antigone, The Handmaid’s Tale, and The Color Purple. *This course may be taken for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT. notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

description: Students in grade 10 may take this course for English credit after successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced, and a referral by their school counselor. The Community Based Learning (CBL) Program is designed to provide active, real world learning experiences for students in grades 10 through 12. The program places students in internships with local businesses and organizations. Students spend four class blocks per week out in the community at their jobs and one block per week in the classroom engaging in academic, English-focused work. Through this program, students explore their professional interests and develop their academic skills. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English.
notes: Open to: 10-12 (Students are referred for this course by their school counselor)

description: This course is for students who have already successfully completed Community Based Learning (CBL) and want to explore a different type of work or to build on previous learning in a repeat placement. Interested students should complete a short application (available in counseling) indicating their motivation for taking the class again, reflection about precious CBL experience, and areas of professional academic interest. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English. Completion of Community Based Learning Program and application, and a referral by their school counselor.
notes: Open to: 11-12 (Students are referred for this course by their School Counselor)

description: This course is for students who have already successfully completed Community Based Learning (CBL) and want a more in-depth work experience. Students will spend 2-3 blocks, back to back, out in the community at their job site four days per week. Additionally, students will spend 2-3 blocks each week engaging in academic, English and career-focused work. Academic work may be focused on a relevant area of research/skill development, entrepreneurship, running a small business, or may be structured as a reading/writing intensive. Academic assignments are co-developed by students and the teacher. Interested students should complete a short application (available in counseling). MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.

notes: Open to: 11-12 (Students are referred for this course by their School Counselor)

description: This course is the closest in structure to the English 1 and 2 College and Career courses. This class provides the opportunity for group and individual study of both traditional and contemporary American authors, and how they reflect and shape American society. Discussion will be an important part of the course, so you’ll need to do what’s necessary to be able to “bring something to the table” each day. Expect reading homework most nights and writing short pieces approximately twice a week. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English.

description: This course is an independent project of the student's choosing. This offering may not duplicate existing courses. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.

description: In this course, students will explore a variety of poetry, look at the various structures and terminology of the genre (such as, but not limited to, foot, meter, rhyme, figurative speech, imagery, literal and figurative meaning, tone, sound, symbol, and rhythm). Students will also write, share, and critique their own poems in class. In addition, students will read a variety of poetry, respond to the poems and share their reactions in a group setting. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options. Alternates with Creative Writing
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English.

description: In this course, students will explore issues of modern culture including political and literary history, technological progress, the changing shape of information, and cultural identity. Units will revolve around utopian visions of modernity, the consequences of modernism, media and the shape of society, and modern citizenship. There will be a variety of texts and media, including novels and long-form non-fiction. There will be regular reading homework and regular writing assignments. Readings may include such titles as Hamlet, Brave New World, Cat’s Cradle, Feed, and Between the World and Me, as well as a variety of short fiction, articles, poetry, and film. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English.

description: The language of myth is the language of human experience. Students will explore both hero myths and creation myths over the course of civilization. Through a study of cultures and their stories, both ancient and contemporary, we will explore who we are as human beings. The following cultures may be studied: Babylonian, Greek, Roman, Celtic, Norse, Native American, Asian, and African. The primary text used is World Mythology. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English.

description: Students who have completed English 1 and 2 successfully may receive English 3 or 4 credit for this course. VPAA students in grade 10 (accepted into the course via instructor permission only; grade 11 is preferred for all students) will receive general elective credit. This is a performance-oriented program for students who wish to learn more about acting and the theatre profession. No previous acting experience is required, but students must be willing to take risks and criticism as part of the creative process. Students will learn how to interpret text and develop believable characters. The course will also include units in auditioning, acting for the camera, make-up, and theatre history. Students are required to attend a variety of off-site productions and field-based learning experiences. A significant amount of reading and written work will be required along with “performance-based” assignments. MAY NOT be taken concurrently (for English Credit) with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English. and permission of the instructor.
fulfills_text: Students who have completed English 1 and 2 successfully may receive English 3 or 4 credit for this course.

description: Students who have completed English 1 and 2 successfully will receive English 3 or 4 credit for this course. VPAA students in grade 10 (accepted into the course via instructor permission only; grade 11 is preferred for all students) will receive general elective credit. This is a rigorous academic course for students who wish to learn more about directing for the stage and other technical aspects of theatre production. Previous acting experience is highly recommended as students will both direct and act with classmates in a number of directing exercises and scenes. Active daily participation if required. Students must be eager to take creative risks and to receive critical feedback on their work. Students write major essays, a research paper, frequent short reviews, and prepare a director’s prompt book. MAY NOT be taken concurrently (for English Credit) with any first or second course options.

description: VPA theatre students must take either this course or the VPA Capstone Directing Showcase. They are encouraged to take both. This course offers students planning to audition for theatre schools the opportunity to: ● Investigate audition requirements for schools to which they are applying ● Receive guidance on the preparation of these materials from the instructor ● Receive guidance on audition preparation tips and techniques from the instructor ● Practice the monologues they will have to perform in the auditions ● Put together a “reel” of other work that may be required from the school (s) of their choice Upon completion of the course of study, some form of public performance or portfolio will be required. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.

notes: Open to: VPA Theatre seniors or other seniors planning to audition for college theatre schools. Seniors only.

description: VPA theatre students must take either this course or the VPA Capstone: Audition Prep. They are encouraged to take both. This course offers students to prepare and present a one-act play or scene from a full-length play of their choice in the spring. The course will take them through the process of: ● Preparing the script for auditions and rehearsals, resulting in a director’s prompt book ● Arranging for costumes, props, and set pieces ● Arranging venues for rehearsals and the performance ● Advertising and writing a press release ● Preparing a printed program ● Arranging logistics for the performance ● Reflecting on the experience MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English. Successful completion of both Performing Arts: Acting and Performing Arts: Directing, or permission of instructor.
notes: Open to: VPA theatre seniors or other seniors with a serious interest in theatre. Seniors only.

description: Restorative Justice—or, transformative justice, restorative practices, transformative practices, etc.—is a concept as old as the human community itself. Often contrasted against contemporary criminal justice, with its emphasis on punishment and isolation, restorative justice seeks to address harm, provide restitution and vindication to those harmed, and, when possible, reintegrate the offender into the community through personal transformation. In short: we all live and work together, and we need each other, and when conflict and offense arises, we seek to heal rather than ignore, condemn, segregate, or punish. In this elective, we will study the origins and practice of restorative justices throughout history and in contemporary society. We will engage in personal and transpersonal practices aimed at re-imagining our roles and relationships as members of the community. Students will examine individual historical situations where restorative justice was or could have been employed, and students will develop transformative justice plans based on real and imagined circumstances. Finally, students will focus on one or several aspects of the approach and historical context as the basis of a research paper and presentation. Students in this class will be invited to engage more deeply with BUHS’s evolving Restorative Justice program, whether participating in circles, developing protocols, or working on peer outreach. Texts may include: The Little Book of Race and Restorative Justice, by Fania E. Davis; selections from Restoring Justice: an Introduction, by Daniel W. Van Ness; selections from The Big Book of Restorative Justice, edited by Howard Zehr. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English.

description: The books we read as children meant one thing to us then, but are worth another look years later. As we read some classic children’s books, we’ll also be reading about the philosophy, psychology, sociology, history, and cultural connections of the books, in addition to literary criticism and film adaptations. This course is designed to mimic a discussion-based college seminar class and is fast-paced. Expect to do annotations, light research, bi-weekly essays, and daily discussions. We will dive deeply into the literature we read and will cover quite a bit of ground during the course. This will be a scholarly look at what seems to be a very simple subject. *This course may be taken for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English.
notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

description: This course introduces students to a variety of advanced speech skills and gives practical exposure to, and experience in, the use of those skills. Students will be required to participate in several different forms of speech presentation, including individual informative and persuasive speeches, discussion groups, debates, interviews, and interpretive readings of literature. Extensive work will be done in the areas of research, subject analysis, problem-solving, persuasion and argumentation, organization, interpretation, and speech delivery. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English.

description: Television Production is designed to encourage students to develop the necessary skills to write, film, and perform all aspects of a television broadcast. In addition, students will learn to program the various technical equipment, film effectively, create special effects, and newscasts, work with Adobe Photoshop to create graphics, edit films using iMovie and FinalCut Pro, and air their broadcasts to the greater Brattleboro community. The students will be responsible for creating and airing a live broadcast at least three times a week. In addition to the broadcasts, students will compose short films, commercials, and documentaries and will also be expected to film school events such as sports games. Students in this class must be motivated and self-directed with the ability to adapt to unexpected change. They must also be able to work closely as part of a team. Solid communication skills (public speaking, reading, and writing), and strong computer skills are strongly recommended. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Interview with the teacher. (Computer skills are also helpful).

description: Production of grade 80 or better. Television Production 2 is designed to encourage students to develop their interests in video production for BUHS television. Students are required to submit a final video portfolio featuring work completed in TV and TV 2. Students work closely with TV 1 students and assist in the daily broadcast. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English. Television

description: In this upperclassman elective, students will engage in research and produce comprehensive papers in three major academic formats: MLA (Modern Language Association), APA (American Psychological Association), and CMS (Chicago Manual of Style). The instructor places emphasis on research methods, organization and construction, and revision. Much of this class is student-driven—half of each week will be spent working independently on research (reading, researching, note-taking, or composing); while the instructor is available to advise, assist, and direct, completion of this course is contingent on students’ ability to manage time, material, and long-term plans. Students will need to undertake a substantial amount of reading and composition outside class in order to achieve our goals. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English.

description: This course requires students to submit a completed course contract and to complete substantial pre-course assignments. Students who complete this course are also required to take the corresponding Advanced Placement English Language and Composition exam in May. This course was designed according to guidelines set by the Advanced Placement Program of the College Board. This course engages students in becoming skilled readers of prose written in a variety of periods, disciplines, and contexts. Students become skilled writers who compose for a variety of purposes and in a variety of forms: narrative, exploratory, expository, argumentative, and on a variety of subjects from personal experiences to public policy, from imaginative literature to popular culture. The overarching purpose is to enable students to read complex texts with understanding and to write prose of sufficient richness and complexity to communicate with mature readers. Readings may include: Friday Night Lights, Narrative of Frederick Douglass, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, 1984, Nickel and Dimed and Into the Wild, in addition to articles, short stories, poems, and speeches for stylistic analysis. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English

description: Students in this course will read, analyze, and create literature in three different genres: poetry, short fiction, and personal essay. There is an emphasis on vocabulary, peer editing, and revision. Students who enroll should be prepared to read and write responses to peer work weekly, to work in small workshop groups, and to engage in bold experimentation with their own craft; as such, this is a course for brave students who love literature, art, and discussion. Alternates with Intro to Poetry MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and second course in English

description: This semester-long elective course will utilize sports as a lens to look deeply into human nature and culture. Examining texts about competition, spectacle, personal struggle, and personal triumph, we will consider the positive themes of heroism, pride, leadership, and identity and the negative themes of disappointment, corruption, scandal, racism, sexism, and misuse of power. Literature may be chosen from among the following texts: The Boys in the Boat, Born to Run, Shoeless Joe, Little Girls in Pretty Boxes, Friday Night Lights, The Crossover, Furia, In These Girls Hope is a Muscle, Gym Candy, as well as poems, short stories, current articles, and films. (THIS COURSE ALTERNATES WITH ADVENTURE READING) MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English.

description: Students enrolled in this course receive instruction in language and academic learning strategies for student success. The course supports development of academic language skills (listening, reading, speaking and writing) in the areas of mathematics, science, social studies, ELA and general instruction. Students analyze similarities in language expectations across these content areas, and develop proficiency across them. An emphasis on post-secondary planning and career options is interwoven into this applied-learning class.
notes: Credit value taken from department introduction (p.34): "ELL Content Support (2 credits)"

description: This course highlights skills, and language needed to add English as a New Language. Using the theme of Community, students work on beginning English skills, introduction to literacy, and phonemic awareness. A strong emphasis is placed on orientation to school systems and communities for social-cultural adjustment.
notes: ELL course for the WIDA proficiency level named in the title

description: This course builds on foundational knowledge in Entering English to increase communicative competence beyond basic English proficiency into a wider array of language tasks and skills. Students at this level have mastered the state standards for Entering level. Students at Emerging Level build vocabulary and literacy skills, using a reading series based on progressively difficult text. They begin to work with formal grammar points, precise vocabulary, and idioms. Students learn to format paragraphs, letters, and short oral presentations after cooperative group projects.
notes: ELL course for the WIDA proficiency level named in the title

description: Building on foundational skills in the first two English Proficiency Levels, the Developing course, increases the diversity of language skills, technical vocabulary, and uses of language across a wide range of topics and content areas. A priority is placed on building academic literacy in English, relying on students’ strengths in other proficiency areas. Students are introduced to a wide variety of communication genres including informational text, expository writing, poetry, narratives, and autobiographies.
notes: ELL course for the WIDA proficiency level named in the title

description: This class focuses on refining language and expression through advanced English language experiences across a wide range of content areas for English development. Advanced grammar and vocabulary study are woven into the curriculum, which often focuses on exploring post-secondary options and planning for the future. Increased independent and project-based learning, allow for individualized study and language development according to student goals. Reading and writing of extensive expository and fictional text are part of the language experience.
notes: ELL course for the WIDA proficiency level named in the title

description: This class prepares students to meet exit criteria from the ELL program. It works with advanced language topics and projects to develop full proficiency in English. Projects may include advanced vocabulary and grammar study, and analysis of fiction and nonfiction texts. Research reports and English projects for a wide variety of purposes continue to support the language acquisition process to ideally support students' multilingualism to the maximum benefit to the learner.
notes: ELL course for the WIDA proficiency level named in the title

description: This course emphasizes the conceptual skills of Algebra. Special attention is given to the abstract developmental structure of mathematics and to the student acquiring problem solving skills to be both applied and used as a learning strategy.
prerequisites: Recommendation of Current Teacher
notes: Catalog level: Level 1 accelerated sequence (p.35)

description: This course consists of a Euclidean approach to plane and solid geometry. Emphasis is placed on deductive reasoning and formal proof using postulates, definitions, and theorems. Methods of inductive reasoning are explored through the use of dynamic geometry software.
prerequisites: 80 or better in Accelerated Algebra 1 or recommendation of Algebra 1 teacher
notes: Catalog level: Level 1 accelerated sequence (p.35)

description: This course is a continuation of Accelerated Algebra One. Topics include graphing systems of linear equations and a graphical analysis of higher order polynomials. The student studies manipulation of algebraic expressions, particularly those containing rational exponents and radicals. *This course may also be offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
prerequisites: 80 or better in Accelerated Algebra 1
notes: Catalog level: Level 1 accelerated sequence (p.35). Catalog notes this course may also be offered for college credit (see DUAL ENROLLMENT)

description: This course prepares students for, and is the principal prerequisite for, AP calculus. The student studies elementary functions including: transformations, combinations of functions, inverse functions, polynomial, exponential, logarithmic, rational and trigonometric functions with an emphasis on their unifying properties. Sinusoidal functions and oblique triangle trigonometry are studied in depth. Literal derivation of basic formulas, individual and group projects, and problem solving are key components of this course. It is assumed that a student taking this course is self- motivated and genuinely interested in an exploratory approach to learning mathematics. The level of success students will experience in this course is directly related to how well they have internalized the skills and concepts studied in their previous mathematics courses.
prerequisites: 80 or better in Accelerated Algebra 2 and Accelerated Geometry
notes: Catalog level: Level 1 accelerated sequence (p.35)

description: Statistics is an introduction to the basic ideas and techniques of probability and statistics. Topics included are: numerical and graphical descriptive measures, probability, random variables, probability distributions (binomial, geometric and the normal), sampling theory, estimation and confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, use of the correlation coefficient in making predictions from regression equations (both linear and nonlinear). Numerical calculations of the above will be done using technology. *This course may also be offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
prerequisites: 75 or better in Algebra 2
notes: Catalog notes this course may also be offered for college credit (see DUAL ENROLLMENT)

description: A college level course in differential and integral calculus which was designed according to guidelines set by the Advanced Placement Program of the College Board. Prepares the student for the Calculus AB Advanced Placement Examination.
prerequisites: 80 or better in Accelerated Pre-Calculus

description: A standard beginning Algebra course consisting of properties of real numbers; solving linear equations and inequalities; graphing linear functions; writing linear equations to solve word problems; solving systems of linear equations, exponential functions and data and statistics.
prerequisites: Teacher recommendation

description: This course offers a Euclidean approach to plane geometry which includes a study of the properties of polygons, (especially triangles and quadrilaterals), parallelism, perpendicularity, and circles. The student also studies the concepts and applications of congruence, similarity, and coordinate geometry.
prerequisites: 75% or better in Algebra 1

description: This course is a continuation of Algebra One. The student studies the applications of the real number system to solving second degree equations, factoring polynomials and solving exponential functions using logarithms. Topics include graphing with an emphasis on solving systems of equations and quadratics. Students interested in taking this course who do not meet the prerequisite criteria above should consult with their previous math teacher and counselor.
prerequisites: 75% or better in Algebra 1

description: In this course the student will be exposed to functions including, polynomial, exponential, logarithmic, rational, and trigonometric. Students will study the parent function and shifts that can be applied to the parent function as well as the inverses of these functions and their applications in real world situations. Personal ownership of a scientific calculator is highly recommended for students taking this course. Students interested in taking this course who do not meet the prerequisite criteria above should consult with their previous math teacher and counselor.
prerequisites: 75% or better in Algebra 1 and Geometry

description: This is an introductory course intended to prepare students for Algebra. Emphasis is placed on covering the most fundamental standard in the Common Core State Standards in mathematics. The pace of the course is adjusted so that careful attention can be given to reinforcing skills necessary for success in future math courses. Content standards will focus on: Ratios and Proportional Relationships, The Number System, Expressions And Equations, Functions, Geometry, Statistics and Probability.
prerequisites: Teacher recommendation

description: This course is designed to help students develop the knowledge and skills necessary to make sound personal financial decisions. Exploring the importance of a budget, learning to maintain a savings plan, realizing the importance of investing and planning for retirement, and managing risk. Students will recognize the importance of taking responsibility for their own financial well-being and examine how their daily decisions around money affect their future financial success.
prerequisites: Algebra 1 and any Geometry

course_name: Intro to Coding and Computer Science
description: Students taking Introduction to Coding and Computer Science will learn the foundations of computer science and coding using the Javascript language. The course allows students to build understanding of variables, data types, logical operators, conditional statements, loops, arrays, and functions, using an engaging, highly graphical coding environment.
prerequisites: Algebra 1 and Geometry with a grade of 75 or above or with department head approval.

description: The student will acquire the basic skills of mathematics through the discovery and application of problem solving strategies. The student will also acquire the ability to communicate mathematically, both orally and in writing and should expect to work collaboratively with fellow students in small groups, and to make class presentations. Topics may include: probability, tessellation and other geometric concepts, logical reasoning, drawings and diagrams, coordinate geometry, and algebra. There will be high expectations for in-class participation and productivity.
prerequisites: Algebra 1 and Geometry

description: An independent project of the student’s choosing. This offering is not intended to duplicate existing courses and is not eligible for core credit. Content should be determined in consultation with the Mathematics Department as early as possible. The student must find a faculty mentor to monitor this study
prerequisites: With the approval of the head of the mathematics department

description: The required first course in the BUHS Science sequence provides students with a study of Earth and its place in the universe. Topics may include: the history of Earth, plate tectonics, weathering, erosion and deposition, climate, space systems and human sustainability. The common thread is how everything changes over time. We will connect what we learn to issues of human impact, climate change and sustainability. How are we humans changing our planet?
fulfills_text: The required first course in the BUHS Science sequence

description: Students are introduced to fundamental concepts of biology including biochemistry, the living cell, characteristics of life, evolution and genetics. A variety of lab exercises and problem solving activities will be used to demonstrate these principles. A term project, the Capstone, presented by the student to the class, may be a culmination of student research and understanding
prerequisites: Successful completion of ESS
fulfills_text: 2nd Required

description: This course is designed to provide students with a background in physical science in a lab-based setting. Students will gain an understanding of the fundamental concepts of matter and its interactions. Topics may include energy, waves, and electricity and magnetism. Students who complete Introduction to Chemistry and Physics may continue on to take all 4th and beyond science courses. Students wanting to take AP Physics after taking the Fundamentals of Chemistry and Physics, should first take either a full semester of Chemistry or Physics.
prerequisites: Successful completion of ESS and Biology
fulfills_text: 3rd Required (Introduction to Chemistry and Physics, or Chemistry or Physics)

description: Physics is a college preparatory course that will probe the fundamental laws of nature which serve as a foundation of all natural phenomena. This course will offer a traditional, mathematically and conceptually based study of classical mechanics, force, motion, energy, thermodynamics, wave motion and light or electricity and magnetism. Historical background of natural philosophy as related to physics will also be included. Students are expected to solve problems, do laboratory work, maintain an organized science notebook , and display effective work and study habits.
prerequisites: Successful completion of ESS and Biology; completed Algebra 2 with 80% or higher or recommendation of Algebra & Biology teachers
fulfills_text: 3rd Required (Introduction to Chemistry and Physics, or Chemistry or Physics)

description: Chemistry is a math-based physical science course designed for students planning to attend college with the possibility of majoring in a science. The course requires excellent study skills, time management, and the use of a scientific calculator in solving problems. Students entering Chemistry are expected to use algebra with minimal review. Chemistry has a strong laboratory component. Students may be required to develop and maintain a science laboratory notebook. Portions of the lab program support student participation in lab design using logical problem solving skills. Topics may include: a review of matter and scientific measurement, quantum mechanics and the periodic table, chemical bonding and chemical reactions, the mole and stoichiometry, the behavior of gasses, solutions chemistry, acid-base chemistry, oxidation-reduction reactions, and thermochemistry. A term project will be required of all Chemistry students.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra 1, ESS and Biology with 80% or higher
fulfills_text: 3rd Required (Introduction to Chemistry and Physics, or Chemistry or Physics)

description: The full-year AP Physics sequence would be an excellent background for students interested in pursuing science, engineering, medical, or related majors in college. The purpose of this course is for students to learn college level physics content with high school support as well as to prepare for success to prepare for the College Board’s AP Physics exam. AP Physics topics will include kinematics, dynamics, work and energy, and gravitation, rotation and fluids. Demonstrated ability in algebra techniques is required. Students will be expected to work at a high academic level at a rapid pace in problem solving, laboratory investigations, and independently directed project work. Students are required to take the AP Physics 1 exam in the spring and complete a design project following the exam.
prerequisites: Application process through Science Department; Pre-Calculus, and 3 science courses (Students who have completed Accelerated Algebra II with an 85% may take AP Physics while taking Pre-Calc.)
fulfills_text: NOTE: While electives within the science department may sometimes be taken out of sequence they do NOT serve as Science graduation requirements with the exception of AP Physics.

description: Wildlife Ecology and Management is a course about the ecology and wildlife of New England. Areas of Study include population dynamics, forest management, aquatic ecology, fisheries management, wildlife management and the natural history of species found in New England. Students enrolled in this course will be expected to participate in field work on a regular basis. Students will be expected to work independently and cooperatively on field studies and projects.
prerequisites: Successful completion of ESS and Biology
fulfills_text: This course is an elective and will not count toward BUHS Science Graduation Requirements.

description: This elective course provides students with a neuroscience-based introduction to core themes in psychology, including sensation and perception, the neuroscience of memory, emotions, and behavior, and the diagnosis and treatment of psychological disorders. Students will need to work effectively both independently and in groups. Lab activities will be an important part of our learning. A term project may be a culmination of student research and understanding.
prerequisites: Successful completion of ESS and Biology
fulfills_text: This course is an elective and will not count toward BUHS Science Graduation Requirements.

description: This course is a Science Department offering open to all grade levels with a particular focus on ninth and tenth grade students who may wish to continue their studies in Environmental Science at BUHS. Students will use the Next Generation Science and Engineering Practices to study real world problems, engaging critical thinking skills to analyze these challenges and formulate solutions. Topic areas will include: how climate has influenced human settlement over time and how humans are now impacting Earth systems; natural resource management and sustainability; forecasting the impacts of climate change; and how we can reduce the effects of human impact through mitigation and adaptation.
fulfills_text: This course is an elective course and does not count toward BUHS Science Graduation Requirements.

description: This course is a Science Department offering to students of all grade levels with the caveat that only students proficient in Algebra 1 and Geometry will have the necessary skills for this course. This course will offer a mathematical and conceptual understanding of orbital dynamics, stellar fusion, and cosmology along with an overview of solar system environments. An historical background of the discovery and exploration of space will also be included. Students are expected to solve problems, complete laboratory work, use computational thinking, and create an engineering design project. Through the comparison of different planetary environments, we will investigate the climate crisis on Earth. This course will provide cross-disciplinary earth science, physical science, life science, and science and engineering practices.
prerequisites: Passed Algebra I and Geometry with an 85 or better, or by permission of a math teacher; Successful completion of ESS.
fulfills_text: This course is an elective and will not count toward BUHS Science Graduation Requirements.

description: Chemistry, or Physics is preferred but students may take these concurrently with your Biology teacher’s recommendation. This course is an elective and will not count toward BUHS Science Graduation Requirements. Advanced Biology is a course for college-bound seniors who have excelled in Biology and previous science course work and are motivated to pursue detailed study in the biological sciences. The focus of this course is the human body and will serve as an excellent preparation for later studies in anatomy and physiology. Human Impact will be studied as relates to human health and disease. The complementarity of structure and function (anatomy and physiology) is a central component of the course which includes opportunities for several dissections. A significant portion of time will be devoted to laboratory activities, problem solving, and group discussion and student presentations. A significant amount of work will be expected outside of class in order to be prepared for laboratory work and seminar discussions within the class
prerequisites: Successful completion of Earth and Space Science, and Biology. Successful completion of IPC,

prerequisites: Three Science courses and extensive interest and initiative. Arrangements must be made with a science instructor with permission of the head of the science department.
fulfills_text: This course is an elective and will not count toward BUHS Science Graduation Requirements.

description: Environmental Science and Policy is an intensive, interdisciplinary course that emphasizes ecosystems, resource use, human population, energy use, climate and agriculture. We study the policies and history that drive how these topics play out in America and worldwide. Students in ES&P work hard to discern the truth in these ever-controversial topics, looking at data, its interpretation and its sources. Environmental Science and Policy is a reading and writing intensive course that draws exclusively from college level material. A willingness and commitment to working hard is necessary for success in this rigorous course. *This course may also be offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
prerequisites: Honors level work in ESS, Biology, Introduction to Chemistry and Physics, or either Chemistry or Physics and teacher recommendation.
fulfills_text: This course is an elective and will not count toward BUHS Science Graduation Requirements.

description: An examination of the culture, geography, and history in world culture regions aligned with the Common Core State Standards. While learning about our changing world, the student will be better informed about the dynamics of the earth/human situation, will strengthen existing Social Studies skills, and will begin to develop a global perspective on the present and the future. Students can expect a variety of learning activities in the course which will include discussions, lectures, written assignments, audio-visual experiences, map work, simulation/games, debates, and personal contact with people of other cultures. World Cultures and Geography meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.
fulfills_text: World Cultures and Geography meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.

description: In this political science course students will examine global political structures, institutions and systems. Using the comparative method, students will compare and contrast the political structures of several different states. They will develop the skills to compare and contrast the nature of these states and will use current political events to enhance their understanding. Some of the themes and concepts under study will include: political ideologies, systems of government, international relations, international political organizations, development and underdevelopment, civil society, power, sovereignty, citizenship, economic systems and public policy. Comparative Politics and Current Events meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.
fulfills_text: Comparative Politics and Current Events meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.

description: This is an interdisciplinary course that helps students to identify and respond to issues of bias and discrimination in society. It combines history and civics content. Students will learn about the social, political, and economic structures in society, including why they were designed and who they benefit. Students will also learn about different ways that individuals and groups have created change within society. The course is designed to help students become active and engaged participants in society. Diversity, Equity, and Civic Action meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.
prerequisites: World Cultures and Geography or Comparative Politics
fulfills_text: Diversity, Equity, and Civic Action meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.

course_name: United States in the World 1 1870 to 1945
description: A survey of the social, political and economic history of Vermont, the United States, and the World from 1870 through 1945 aligned with the Common Core State Standards. Teachers will strive to relate historical events in perspective to contemporary issues. Emphasis is placed on writing, study skills and critical thinking as well as the development of concepts related to history and social studies. A wide variety of teaching materials and methods are applied throughout the course. Students will be asked to conduct personal research as well as maintain knowledge of contemporary events. US in the World 1: 1870 to 1945 meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.
prerequisites: One of the 9th grade options and Diversity, Equity, and Civic Action

course_name: United States in the World 2 1945 to Present
description: A survey of the social, political and economic history of Vermont, the United States, and the World from 1945 to the present, aligned with the Common Core State Standards. Teachers will strive to relate historical events in perspective to contemporary issues. Emphasis is placed on writing, study skills and critical thinking as well as the development of concepts related to history and social studies. A wide variety of teaching materials and methods are applied throughout the course. Students will be asked to conduct personal research as well as maintain knowledge of contemporary events. US in the World 2: 1945 to the Present meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.
prerequisites: One of the 9th grade options and Diversity, Equity, and Civic Action
fulfills_text: US in the World 2: 1945 to the Present meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.

course_name: Social Studies Seminar: Black American History
description: This course is a comprehensive exploration of the rich and complex history of Black Americans. It delves into the multifaceted experiences of Black people in the United States, from the era of enslavement to the 20th century. By examining the economic, social, political, and cultural contributions of Black Americans, students will gain a deeper understanding of their impact on American history. By the end of this course, students will have a nuanced understanding of the historical experiences of Black Americans and their enduring contributions to American society.
prerequisites: Successful completion of three required social studies courses

description: The AP U.S. History course focuses on developing students’ understanding of American history from approximately 1491 to the present. The course has students investigate the content of U.S. history for significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in nine historical periods, and develop and use the same thinking skills and methods (analyzing primary and secondary sources, making historical comparisons, chronological reasoning, and argumentation) employed by historians when they study the past. The course also provides seven themes (American and national identity; migration and settlement; politics and power; work, exchange, and technology; America in the world; geography and the environment; and culture and society) that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places. College Course Equivalent AP U.S. History is designed to be the equivalent of a two-semester introductory college or university U.S. history course. Students electing this course will be required to take the AP U.S. History exam. AP US History meets a social studies school requirement for graduation. Advanced Placement United States History will count as meeting 8 credit requirements.
prerequisites: Completion of English 1 and 2 and Completion of Diversity, Equity, and Civic Action

description: The course provides an introductory study of sociology using the principles and methods of social sciences and the scientific method. Sociological principles, sociological perspectives, and the relationship of the individual to societal groups will be emphasized. Culture and the elements influencing society today are major themes of the course. Other topics that will be examined include socialization, social structure, stratification, race, class, family, education, population, economics, religion, gender, age, and social change. Sociological research and the role of sociologists in the modern world are discussed. Students learn to think critically about the nature of society and social institutions. Large and small group discussion is emphasized. A number of papers will also be required

description: This dual-credit course is an overview of constitutional, criminal, and civil law. The course emphasizes active citizenship and the balance between individual liberties and security. Learning will be facilitated through discussion, group work, simulations, case studies, research, presentations, guest speakers, and independent projects. All students will have the option of engaging in an internship or project out in the community. In addition, the class will take part in field studies at the District Court of Vermont and at the Southern Vermont Correctional Facility. The class makes use of a wide variety of materials, including various texts, readings, videos, periodicals, and internet resources. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.

description: The ability to mentor is a valued competency in business, non-profit, academic, civic and team environments. This course is intended to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of concepts, principles and practice of mentoring through theoretical and practical applications. Students will develop the necessary knowledge and skills needed to foster or create and maintain effective mentoring relationships. Topics include: creating mentoring relationships, stages of mentoring, understanding learning styles; working with groups vs. individuals and managing difficult conversations. A major component of this course will be field work in which students will be expected to select a mentoring project. Examples include: developing programs for students transitioning into BUHS, middle school leadership teams and Big Brothers/Big Sisters. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
prerequisites: Successful completion of three required social studies courses
notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

description: This course provides a foundation in the basic concepts upon which our economic system operates. Students study current economic issues and problems as they relate to producers, consumers, government, labor, management, and finance. Extensive reading, research, and writing are course expectations. Special emphasis is given to the examination and development of economic case studies resulting in students-designed case studies. In addition, class activities include seminars, group work, lectures, simulations, and presentations by guest speakers and student use of the Internet to obtain current data and research materials. Assessment of progress is based on the analysis of class participation, research, homework, quizzes, and tests. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
prerequisites: Successful completion of three required social studies courses

course_name: U.S. History Through Film and Music
description: The US History Through Film and Music course will offer students a different way to explore themes of US history through the lens of film and music. Students will learn how to critically analyze film and music, while gaining new insight into historical events of the 18th, 19th and 20th Centuries. This class will require students to work collaboratively both in discussion groups and on projects, as well as to complete independent writing.
prerequisites: Successful completion of three required social studies courses

description: This course focuses on the election process and the way in which local, state, and national government is organized. A key element of this course is the requirement that students become active participants in the events and activities of an election campaign or by direct involvement in government services. Special features of this class include presentations by candidates, elected and appointed government officials, and the media. Students are accountable for completion of reading, research and writing activities both in and out of class. When feasible, field studies are conducted to provide exposure to the activities of government. Assessment of progress is based on the analysis of completed assignments, class participation, research, quizzes and tests . *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
prerequisites: Successful completion of three required social studies courses

description: This two-credit course examines the American Revolution and the Civil War, with a particular focus on the political and philosophical developments that led to the Revolution, key military turning points, debates over government and representation, and the Revolution's impact from the late 18th century to the present. The course concludes by exploring how unresolved conflicts over slavery and citizenship during the Revolutionary period led to the outbreak of the American Civil War. Students will be empowered to think critically about questions of power, government, human rights, representation, and how historical events continue to shape the country today.

The 20th Century has been called a century of genocide. Why? This course will explore five genocides that occurred in the last century. Beginning with a half semester spent on the study of the Holocaust students will use personal testimonies, literature, research, and video to gather a full understanding of the causes and effects of the Holocaust. The second half of the semester will be spent exploring and comparing the cause and effects of genocides in the Ottoman Empire, Cambodia, Bosnia, and Rwanda. Much of the class depends on student discussion, participation, reading, writing and research. There will be opportunities to attend events outside of BUHS. * This course may also be offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.

description: Students in Latin I are introduced to basic Latin vocabulary and grammar through direct readings in Latin, using the textbook Lingua Latina Per Se Illustrata. These readings focus on the daily life of a typical upper-class Roman family in the second century A.D. Latin I students begin to make linguistic connections to English and other modern languages. In addition to studying the language itself, students also begin to learn about Roman history and culture. Themes: Themes explored in Latin 1 include the provinces of the Roman Empire, daily life, family roles, slavery, the structure of a Roman house, travel in the Ancient World, and Roman mythology.

Students in Latin II develop and expand their Latin skills through direct readings in Latin, using the textbook Lingua Latina Per Se Illustrata. Latin II students continue to make linguistic connections to English and other modern languages. In addition to studying the language itself, students also continue to learn about Roman history and culture. Themes: Themes explored in Latin II include animals, medicine, the military, the Roman calendar, education, sea travel, and advanced numbers and letters.

Students in Latin III continue to develop and expand their Latin skills through direct readings in Latin, using the textbook Lingua Latina Per Se Illustrata. Latin III students continue to make linguistic connections to English and other modern languages. In addition to studying the language itself, students also continue to learn about Roman history and culture. Themes: Themes explored in Latin III include marriage and childbirth, medicine, Roman government, dinner parties, and mythology.

Students in Latin IV begin to read authentic Latin texts from the Ancient Roman world, with a focus on Latin inscriptions and poetry. While reading these texts, students continue to develop and expand their Latin skills, make linguistic connections to English and other modern languages, and learn about Roman history and culture. Themes: Themes explored in Latin IV include Latin inscriptions from the Roman world, and the poetry of Catullus and Martial.

While this class serves as a foundation gateway class it is geared more towards the practical arts than the fine arts. If you like working with your hands, this is a good class for you. description: Studio Art Drawing is an intermediate course focusing on drawing and design skills. Students will be exposed to a range of media and techniques to enhance their skills. A strong emphasis is also placed on composition. Students who have completed Foundations in Art or who have a waiver based on a submitted portfolio of drawing may qualify for the class. All abilities are welcome and evaluation is based on student improvement over the course of the semester vs. innate talent. This is predominantly a “hands on” class and also explores art history through presentations and web journeys. Portfolio development is supported.
prerequisites: Foundations of Art (Traditional class)

description: An intermediate course focused on developing an understanding of paint and color. Students will explore color through a variety of materials and techniques. While predominantly a “hands on” course, students will increase their understanding of color theory, art history, and composition, and be asked to respond to art through reading and writing. A partial list of materials may include pastel, watercolor, acrylic paint, and mixed media. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
prerequisites: Studio Art 1 (Drawing and Design)
notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

description: Ceramics are used throughout the world in myriad cultures for both their function and their form. Through hands-on projects students will develop patience and discipline while working with clay. Ceramic projects take a long time to complete from wet clay through two firings to a finished piece. This course requires students to balance production of multiple projects with good studio practice. Clay is a messy medium and students are required to maintain studio cleanliness; they will be given chores to help do so. The first half of the course is structured around developing skills with different techniques used to manipulate clay (e.g. slab building, coiling, sculpting, coiling, etc). The second half of the course is structured around artistic problems or questions that require students to think about the design, function, and aesthetics that they will use to solve the problem(s) posed. There is a lab fee of $10.00, which students are expected to pay. This fee helps to partially cover material, firing, and maintenance costs. Finances are different for everyone and if you have concerns you may talk to the teacher or to counseling if you are more comfortable. We may decide to waive the fee.
prerequisites: Strongly recommend Foundations (Traditional class)

description: This course offers disciplined and motivated students the opportunity to continue to develop skills in different techniques working with clay through hands-on projects. Students will be presented with artistic questions which they will have to explore through the medium of clay. The second part of the course is designated for students to work independently to develop their own series of work with a written artist statement to accompany it. There is a lab fee of $10.00, which students are expected to pay. This fee helps to partially cover material, firing, and maintenance costs. Finances are different for everyone and if you have concerns you may talk to the teacher or to counseling if you are more comfortable. We may decide to waive the fee. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
prerequisites: Ceramics 1 with a grade of 75 or above or with department head approval.
notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

description: This advanced course is tailored for self-motivated and disciplined students eager to elevate their proficiency in clay artistry through diverse techniques and hands-on projects. Emphasizing autonomy and creative exploration, students will grapple with profound artistic inquiries, using clay as a dynamic medium for expression. In the latter part of the course, students are empowered to chart their own artistic trajectory, developing a personalized series of work alongside a comprehensive written artist statement. This innovative approach encourages students to shape their unique vision within the realm of clay art. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
prerequisites: Ceramics 2 with a grade of 75 or above or with department head approval.
notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

description: Sculpture an intermediate level art class, allows students who have completed Foundations in Art to continue to work on 3 dimensional design problems. The assignments and materials provide a greater challenge than Foundations in Art, and students are given more creative freedom within the assignment framework. In keeping with the departmental philosophy, Sculpture is a discipline based art program in which students learn design theory, art history relevant to their work, and are required to think critically about their work. Various sculptural processes such as casting, relief sculpture, subtractive and additive processes are undertaken and some materials include wood, plaster, clay, and wire. While predominantly a "hands on" course, students will be asked to respond to art through reading and writing. Students will be expected to pay a $10 lab fee at the beginning of the course.
prerequisites: Strongly recommend Foundations of Art (traditional class) or Art of Crafts

description: This course is designed to build on the 3-dimensional design skills learned in Sculpture I and to create at an advanced level. Students will utilize their prior knowledge of color and surface quality, the work of great sculptors past and present, and technical skills to work “in the round” and relief. Casting, multi- piece molds, additive and subtractive methods will be part of the Sculpture II curriculum. Students will have the opportunity to work in teams to create public art that enhances the community. In addition to the creation of sculpture, students are expected to articulate their knowledge and experience through writing and class discussions. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
prerequisites: Fine and Practical Art course and Sculpture I with a grade of 75 or above or with department head approval.
notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

description: This course is a fusion of fiber art, fabrics and fashion. This course is geared towards beginning students’ exposure to technical knowledge in sewing and supports the artist sewer in problem solving creative projects. Sewing machine mechanics, accessories, and maintenance are explained and explored. Students will be introduced to many different types of fabrics, pattern making, hand sewing techniques, notions and more. Class time is mainly hands-on project time. This course draws upon the creative side of students to tap into artistic sewing pieces which may use non-traditional materials or non-traditional sewing craft. A wide variety of fabric is available in the classroom in addition to upcycled clothing donations in support of the art department's efforts of reducing environmental impact. This class includes an introductory fashion drawing unit which assists in satisfying the art graduation requirement or a student’s desire to take additional sewing or drawing coursework.
fulfills_text: (Please note this course satisfies the Art graduation requirement)

description: Independence and freedom in project choice will build on your previous learning. This course is for the student who is interested in learning more sewing and fiber art techniques in addition to having more freedom and project choice. As in Sewing 1, class time is largely hands-on with exploration in quilting, applique, knitting, crewel needlepoint and so much more. A wide variety of fabric is available in the classroom in addition to the upcycled clothing donations in support of the art departments’ efforts of reducing environmental impact. Students will learn how to apply their knowledge gained in Sewing 1 as well as complete a unit on fashion design.
prerequisites: Sewing 1

description: Students will learn about creating living environments that meet specific design concepts and needs. Through design projects students will create hands-on projects that relate to interior design alongside the textbook curriculum. Projects will revolve around drafting, furniture arrangement, and how to execute a storyboard for visual presentation. Storyboards will be created both by hand and by digital apps such as Canva. Art concepts covered are the elements of design, principles of design, and the role of color. This class is for the student who likes to take a personal style vision and develop it into a workable living space. Must have basic knowledge of measuring in order to successfully complete required floor plan drawings. This class is a good prerequisite for sewing and general art classes.
fulfills_text: (Please note this course satisfies the Art graduation requirement)

Advanced techniques, materials, and concepts are explored through teacher presented studies and student developed projects. Student expression and independence is encouraged with teacher guidance. Portfolio development, both digitally and through collected work, can be used to facilitate entrance to art schools and related university studies. Techniques include drawing, printmaking, painting, 2D and 3D design, and non-traditional materials. Selected readings in art history and contemporary art will facilitate discussions and written responses. This course may be repeated for credit. *This course may also be offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.

notes: Catalog notes this course may also be offered for college credit (see DUAL ENROLLMENT)

It will also be open to other juniors and seniors who have taken an advanced level of art. The class will heavily focus on portfolio development and strategies to be a successful working artist. The AP class will focus on sustained investigation, experimentation and communication of ideas in 2D and 3D art. It will focus on the development of skills, processes and concepts.
